findings.title: Google credential key is overwritten with the zod SafeParse wrapper object on every token refresh
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns the result of `schema.safeParse(...)`, i.e. an object of the form `{ success: true, data: {...} }`, not the parsed credentials themselves. In `refreshAccessToken` the return value is assigned to `key` and written straight to the DB with `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. The previous code used `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` which returned the plain credential object. After this change every Google Calendar access-token refresh (roughly hourly, regardless of whether credential syncing is enabled) persists `{success: true, data: {access_token, refresh_token, ...}}` as the credential key. The next time the service is constructed, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` fails because `access_token`/`refresh_token` are no longer top-level fields, so the Google Calendar integration becomes permanently broken for that user until they reconnect. The other call sites (Office365, Zoom, Salesforce) correctly use `.data`; this one must too.

findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in the Salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: The new code in `getClient` calls `prisma.credential.update(...)`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (the import list contains only jsforce, rrule, zod, CalEventParser, constants, http-error, logger, types, getAppKeysFromSlug and parseRefreshTokenResponse). This is a TypeScript compile error (`Cannot find name 'prisma'`) and, if it slipped through, a `ReferenceError` at runtime inside the constructor's promise, meaning every `SalesforceCalendarService` instantiation rejects and the Salesforce integration is completely non-functional.

findings.title: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` computed keys evaluate to "[object Object]"; schema strips every field except access_token
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are computed property keys. Calling `.toString()` on a Zod schema object returns the literal string `"[object Object]"`, so both lines define the same key (the second wins) and the schema is effectively `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() })`. There is no `.passthrough()`/`.catchall()`, so when credential sync is enabled every other field in the provider response (expires_in, expiry_date, refresh_token, scope, token_type, instance_url, ...) is silently stripped. Consequences: Zoom computes `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` = NaN (serialised as null), after which `zoomTokenSchema.parse` fails and Zoom breaks; Office365 never updates `expires_in` so the token is treated as expired and re-fetched on every call; Salesforce loses `instance_url`. The comment "Assume that any property with a number is the expiry" describes behaviour that is not implemented. Use `z.object({ access_token: z.string() }).passthrough()` (and an explicit expiry field) instead.

findings.title: Sync branch returns a fetch Response while the fallback returns provider-SDK objects; several apps crash or corrupt credentials in sync mode
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns `fetch(...)`'s `Response` when `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set, but otherwise returns whatever the app-specific `refreshFunction` returns. Callers are written against the fallback shape, so with syncing enabled: Google (`googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 94) reads `res?.data` which is undefined on a `Response`, throws `TypeError`, is swallowed by the catch and silently keeps the expired token; HubSpot (`hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 177) treats the `Response` as a `HubspotToken`, computes `expiryDate = NaN`, stores the `Response` object as the credential key (serialised to roughly `{expiryDate:null}`) and calls `setAccessToken(undefined)`; Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin read `tokenInfo.data.error` on a `Response` and throw. Lark and Webex expect provider-specific envelopes (`{code, data:{refresh_expires_in,...}}`, literal `scope` string) that contradict the comment "The response should only contain the access token and expiry date". The `refreshFunction: () => any` signature hides all of this from the type checker. The sync branch needs to return a shape each caller can consume (or callers need to normalise), and the endpoint contract needs to be documented per app.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin passes the credential id as the user id to the credential-sync endpoint
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, appSlug, userId)` expects the Cal.com user id as its third argument, but `refreshAccessToken` passes `credentialId` (the `Credential.id`), because `biginAuth` only forwards `credential.id`/`credential.key` and not `credential.userId`. With credential sync enabled this posts `calcomUserId=<credentialId>` to the self-hoster's endpoint, so the tokens for an unrelated user (whoever has that numeric user id) are fetched and written into this credential — both a functional failure and a cross-user token leak. `credential.userId` must be threaded through to `refreshAccessToken`.

findings.title: Webhook looks up `appStoreMetadata` by slug, but the map is keyed by app directory name
findings.body: `appStoreMetadata` (from `apps.metadata.generated.ts`) is keyed by the app's directory name (`googlecalendar`, `zoomvideo`, `office365calendar`, `office365video`, `larkcalendar`, ...), not by its slug (`google-calendar`, `zoom`, `office365-calendar`, `msteams`, `lark-calendar`). Indexing it with `app.slug` only works for apps whose dir name happens to equal the slug (hubspot, salesforce, zohocrm, zoho-bigin, webex). For the main apps this PR targets the lookup returns undefined and the endpoint responds 404 "App not found. Ensure that you have the correct app slug" even though the slug is correct, so credentials can never be synced for them. Use `getAppFromSlug(slug)` from `@calcom/app-store/utils` (or search `Object.values(appStoreMetadata)` by `slug`) instead.

findings.title: Zoom refresh uses app identifier "zoomvideo" while the app slug (and webhook) use "zoom"
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo` to the self-hoster's credential-sync endpoint, but the Zoom app's slug/appId everywhere else is `"zoom"` (see `zoomvideo/api/callback.ts` `appId: "zoom"`, and the inbound webhook resolves apps via `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug } })`). A self-hoster keying their endpoint by the slug they push through the webhook will not recognise `zoomvideo`, so Zoom token refresh fails in sync mode. Every other call site passes the real slug (`google-calendar`, `office365-calendar`, `msteams`, `lark-calendar`, ...); this one should pass `"zoom"`.

findings.title: Placeholder string "refresh_token" is injected into parsed token data and persisted, overwriting real refresh tokens
findings.body: When the parsed response lacks `refresh_token`, the function mutates the data to `refresh_token: "refresh_token"`. This runs in both the sync and non-sync branches. In the non-sync Office365 path, `refreshTokenResponseSchema` marks `refresh_token` optional; if Microsoft omits it, the spread `{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }` now replaces the stored, valid refresh token with the literal string, permanently breaking the credential (previously the spread left it untouched). In sync mode the literal is written to the DB for Zoom (`key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token`) and Office365, so if a self-hoster later disables syncing all those credentials are dead. Callers that need a placeholder should handle it themselves; the shared parser should not fabricate credential material.

findings.title: Request to the credential-sync endpoint carries no authentication
findings.body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` as a form body, with no shared-secret header, signature, or other authentication material. The endpoint is expected to return live OAuth access tokens for arbitrary user ids, so the self-hoster has no way (short of network allow-listing) to verify the request originates from their Cal.com instance; anyone who can reach the endpoint can harvest every user's third-party tokens by enumerating ids. The PR already defines `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`/`CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` for the inbound direction; the outbound request should at minimum send the same secret header so the endpoint can authenticate it.

findings.title: Salesforce now hits the token endpoint on every service instantiation and ignores the refreshed token
findings.body: `getClient` (called from the constructor) now unconditionally POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` with the stored refresh token on every `SalesforceCalendarService` construction (every booking, update, delete), with no expiry check. jsforce already refreshes lazily on 401, so this adds a network round-trip and Salesforce API quota usage to every operation. The refreshed `access_token` is then not even used: the `jsforce.Connection` at line 106 is built from `credentialKey.access_token` (the old value), so the extra call only updates the DB. Additionally the success check `response.statusText !== "OK"` is fragile (status text is empty over HTTP/2 and not guaranteed by fetch) — `response.ok` should be used — and this path bypasses `refreshOAuthTokens`, so Salesforce ignores credential-sync mode and will keep calling Salesforce with whatever refresh token is stored (possibly the "refresh_token" placeholder).

findings.title: Invalid body or undecryptable payload produce unhandled exceptions (500) and decrypted keys are stored unvalidated
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a `ZodError` on a malformed body, and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throws on a wrong key, malformed ciphertext or non-JSON plaintext. None of these are caught (the handler is not wrapped in `defaultResponder`/try-catch), so the caller receives a generic 500 instead of a 400 with a useful message, and the self-hoster cannot distinguish a bad payload from a server fault. The decrypted `keys` value is also written to `credential.key` without any shape validation, so a sender bug (e.g. encrypting the wrong object) silently corrupts the user's credential and only surfaces later when the app's credential schema parse fails.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with `!==` rather than a constant-time comparison
findings.body: The secret header is validated with a plain string inequality against `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. String comparison short-circuits on the first mismatching byte, which leaks timing information that can be used to recover the secret byte-by-byte on a network-reachable endpoint. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers (as other webhook handlers in the codebase do) and reject when lengths differ.

findings.title: `findFirst` by userId+appId overwrites an arbitrary credential for apps that allow multiple installs
findings.body: Several apps (e.g. Google Calendar) allow a user to hold multiple credentials for the same `appId`. The webhook selects `findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` with no ordering and updates whichever row comes back, so a sync for one connected account can clobber the keys of a different connected account of the same provider. There is also no uniqueness constraint, so two concurrent webhook calls for a new user/app pair can both take the `create` branch and produce duplicate credentials. The payload should identify the target credential (or the provider account) rather than relying on `findFirst`.

findings.title: No tests for the new webhook endpoint or the shared OAuth refresh helpers
findings.body: The PR adds a new authenticated API route that writes third-party credentials into the DB and two shared helpers (`refreshOAuthTokens`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) that now sit in the token-refresh path of nine integrations, but ships no unit or integration tests (the PR description explicitly states tests were not added or run). Several of the defects in this change — the `[object Object]` schema key, the SafeParse wrapper being stored as the Google credential key, the missing `prisma` import in Salesforce, and the dirName-vs-slug lookup — would have been caught by even a minimal test exercising the webhook with a known slug and a test asserting the shape written to `prisma.credential.update` after a refresh.
